stem: A SysOps administrator needs to create a CloudWatch dashboard that shows the number of HTTP 5xx errors returned by an Application Load Balancer over the past 24 hours. Which ALB metric should be used?

options.label: A
options.text: RejectedConnectionCount counts the number of connections rejected by the ALB due to connection limits, which correlates with 5xx errors during high traffic.

options.label: B
options.text: TargetResponseTime measures the time for targets to respond; when response time exceeds a threshold, the ALB logs a 5xx error that can be counted by this metric.

options.label: C
options.text: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count counts HTTP 5xx errors generated by the load balancer itself (for example, when no healthy targets are available), not errors from the targets.

options.label: D
options.text: HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count counts the number of HTTP 5xx response codes generated by the registered targets, representing application-level server errors.

distractors.C: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count counts errors generated by the ALB itself, not by the application running on the targets; both metrics may be needed for a complete picture.
distractors.B: TargetResponseTime is a latency metric, not an error count metric; high response time may correlate with errors but does not directly count 5xx responses.
distractors.A: RejectedConnectionCount counts connections the ALB refused due to connection limits; these result in 503 errors but are a specific subset, not all 5xx errors.

explanation: ALBs publish two 5xx metrics: HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count (errors from the ALB itself, e.g., no healthy targets, malformed requests) and HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count (5xx errors returned by the backend targets). For monitoring application errors, HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count is the correct metric, as it reflects application-level failures.

stem: A SysOps administrator needs to be alerted when any IAM policy change is made in the account, regardless of which user or service makes the change. What is the most direct implementation?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the CloudTrail log group matching IAM API calls, publish a custom metric, and create a CloudWatch alarm on the metric with an SNS notification.

options.label: B
options.text: Configure CloudTrail to deliver logs to SNS directly; subscribers receive an SNS notification for every management API call made in the account.

options.label: C
options.text: Create an EventBridge rule with an event pattern that matches CloudTrail management events from source aws.iam with eventNames including CreatePolicy, AttachRolePolicy, PutUserPolicy, and similar, routing to an SNS topic.

options.label: D
options.text: Enable AWS Config with the iam-policy-no-statements-with-admin-access rule; Config triggers SNS notifications when any IAM policy with administrator access is created.

distractors.A: CloudWatch Logs metric filter approach requires CloudTrail logs to be sent to CloudWatch Logs and involves more configuration steps; EventBridge directly receives CloudTrail events without additional log forwarding.
distractors.D: The Config rule only checks for admin-access policies; it does not alert on all IAM policy changes.
distractors.B: CloudTrail delivers log file completion notifications to SNS (not per-event), and the notification only indicates a log file was written, not which specific API calls it contains.

explanation: Amazon EventBridge receives all CloudTrail management events automatically. An event pattern matching {source: [aws.iam], detail.eventName: [CreatePolicy, DeletePolicy, AttachRolePolicy, DetachRolePolicy, PutUserPolicy, ...]} triggers the rule for every matching IAM operation. For all IAM changes, you can match on source aws.iam without specifying individual event names.

stem: CloudWatch agent is installed on EC2 instances but memory metrics are not appearing in CloudWatch. The agent is running and CPU metrics from the same agent are visible. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Memory metrics are published with a 5-minute delay by the CloudWatch agent regardless of the configured collection interval; the metrics exist but appear stale in the console.

options.label: B
options.text: Memory metrics require the instance to use a Nitro-based instance type; non-Nitro instances cannot collect memory metrics through the CloudWatch agent.

options.label: C
options.text: The CloudWatch agent configuration file is missing the mem_used_percent or related metrics in the metrics section; memory metrics must be explicitly configured in the agent config, unlike EC2 built-in metrics.

options.label: D
options.text: The IAM role attached to the EC2 instance is missing the cloudwatch:PutMetricData permission for the CWAgent namespace specifically for memory metrics.

distractors.B: CloudWatch agent memory collection works on all instance types; Nitro-based instances provide certain infrastructure advantages but memory metrics are not restricted to them.
distractors.D: cloudwatch:PutMetricData permission applies to all custom metrics published by the agent; if CPU metrics are appearing, the IAM permission is working correctly for all agent metrics.
distractors.A: The CloudWatch agent publishes metrics at the interval configured; there is no built-in 5-minute delay specific to memory metrics.

explanation: Unlike EC2 built-in metrics (CPU, network, disk I/O), memory utilization is not natively available in CloudWatch. The CloudWatch agent collects memory metrics, but they must be explicitly included in the agent's JSON configuration file under the metrics section. If CPU metrics are working but memory metrics are not, the most likely cause is that memory metrics are not in the agent config.

stem: A SysOps administrator needs to set up a notification when an EC2 instance's root EBS volume has less than 10 GB free. The CloudWatch agent is installed and collecting disk metrics. What is the correct alarm configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the disk_free metric in the CWAgent namespace, filtering by path='/' and device matching the root volume, with a threshold of 10 GB (10,737,418,240 bytes).

options.label: B
options.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the built-in EBS VolumeQueueLength metric with a threshold that correlates to 10 GB of remaining free space.

options.label: C
options.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the disk_used_percent metric with a threshold calculated by subtracting 10 GB from the total volume size and converting to a percentage.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the EBS VolumeReadBytes metric; low read bytes indicates the volume is nearly full and triggering read errors.

distractors.B: VolumeQueueLength measures the number of I/O operations queued; it does not reflect disk free space.
distractors.C: disk_used_percent is also valid for this alarm and may be more practical (e.g., alert at 90% used), but disk_free directly measures absolute free space, making it the more precise answer for a GB-based threshold.
distractors.D: VolumeReadBytes measures I/O throughput; it does not correlate with available free space.

explanation: The CloudWatch agent publishes disk_free and disk_used_percent metrics in the CWAgent namespace for each filesystem. To alert when the root volume has less than 10 GB free, create an alarm on disk_free with path='/' (or the root filesystem mount point) with a threshold of 10737418240 (10 GB in bytes). A dimension filter on the device name ensures the alarm targets the correct volume.

stem: A SysOps administrator needs to investigate why an Auto Scaling group scaled out unexpectedly. Which combination of tools provides the most complete picture of what triggered the scale-out?

options.label: A
options.text: Review the CloudWatch Logs for the Auto Scaling service; the scaling decision and reason are written to a dedicated Auto Scaling log group.

options.label: B
options.text: Check the Auto Scaling group Activity History for the scale-out event description, then review the associated CloudWatch alarm history to see when the alarm transitioned to ALARM state and which metric triggered it.

options.label: C
options.text: Check the EC2 console's instance launch history filtered by the Auto Scaling group; the launch reasons are displayed in the Instances section of the console.

options.label: D
options.text: Query CloudTrail for ec2:RunInstances events in the time window of the scale-out; the event details show which alarm caused the instance launch.

distractors.D: CloudTrail logs the RunInstances call but the caller is the Auto Scaling service, not a named alarm; the reason for the launch is not embedded in the CloudTrail event details.
distractors.A: Auto Scaling does not write decision logs to a CloudWatch Logs log group; activity history is accessible through the Auto Scaling API and console.
distractors.C: The EC2 console shows instance state history but does not expose the Auto Scaling scaling reason; the Auto Scaling Activity History is the correct source.

explanation: The Auto Scaling group Activity History contains a detailed description of each scaling event including the reason (e.g., 'a CloudWatch alarm triggered scale out') and the alarm name. Reviewing the CloudWatch alarm state change history for that alarm then shows exactly when and why the alarm transitioned to ALARM state, including which metric and threshold were breached.

stem: A SysOps administrator wants to set up centralized logging from multiple AWS accounts into a single Amazon S3 bucket in a logging account. What is required in the S3 bucket policy?

options.label: A
options.text: The S3 bucket policy in the logging account must grant the source accounts' CloudTrail service principal permission to s3:PutObject on the bucket, scoped to each account's prefix path.

options.label: B
options.text: The logging account must create VPC Peering connections to each source account to enable CloudTrail to deliver logs privately to the centralized S3 bucket.

options.label: C
options.text: The S3 bucket must be public with write-only access enabled; CloudTrail requires public S3 buckets for multi-account log delivery to avoid cross-account permission complexity.

options.label: D
options.text: The source accounts' CloudTrail configurations must use an IAM role that assumes a role in the logging account with S3 write permissions; no bucket policy changes are required in the logging account.

distractors.D: CloudTrail uses the aws-cloudtrail service principal to write to S3; it does not assume a cross-account IAM role for log delivery. The bucket policy must grant the CloudTrail service principal access.
distractors.C: CloudTrail log buckets must never be public; cross-account delivery is handled through resource-based bucket policies, not public access.
distractors.B: S3 is a global service that does not require VPC Peering for cross-account access; bucket policies handle cross-account authorization.

explanation: For centralized CloudTrail logging, the S3 bucket policy in the logging account must allow the aws-cloudtrail.amazonaws.com service principal to perform s3:GetBucketAcl and s3:PutObject. The PutObject permission is scoped to the prefix path that includes each source account ID. For an Organization Trail, you can use the AWS::SourceOrgID condition for additional security.

stem: A SysOps administrator is using AWS Systems Manager Automation to remediate non-compliant resources. The automation document runs successfully in the console but fails when triggered automatically by AWS Config. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The IAM role specified in the Config remediation action does not have sufficient permissions to execute the SSM Automation document or to modify the non-compliant resource.

options.label: B
options.text: AWS Config cannot trigger SSM Automation documents automatically; automated remediation must be invoked manually through the Config console or CLI.

options.label: C
options.text: The SSM Automation document requires the CloudWatch agent to be running on the target resource; Config-triggered remediation fails if the agent is not active.

options.label: D
options.text: Config-triggered automation runs in a different AWS region than the non-compliant resource; cross-region SSM Automation execution is not supported.

distractors.B: AWS Config does support automatic remediation; it is a built-in feature that triggers SSM Automation documents when resources are found non-compliant.
distractors.C: SSM Automation documents execute API calls through the SSM service, not through an agent on the target; the CloudWatch agent status is irrelevant.
distractors.D: Config remediation can target resources in the same region; and SSM Automation can execute cross-region if the document and automation role are configured correctly.

explanation: Config automated remediation requires specifying an IAM role (the 'Automation assume role') that SSM Automation uses to execute the document. This role needs permissions to call SSM StartAutomationExecution and whatever API actions the document performs (e.g., ec2:ModifyInstanceAttribute, s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock). When running manually in the console, the user's permissions are used; when Config triggers it automatically, the specified automation role's permissions apply.

stem: A company uses AWS Health to monitor service disruptions. A SysOps administrator needs to receive Slack notifications when any AWS service affecting the company's account has an issue. What is the correct integration?

options.label: A
options.text: Subscribe to AWS Health RSS feeds in a Lambda function that polls the feed every 5 minutes and posts messages to Slack via the Slack API when new incidents are detected.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable AWS Health third-party integrations in the Personal Health Dashboard settings and enter the Slack webhook URL in the notifications configuration panel.

options.label: C
options.text: Create an EventBridge rule that matches events from source aws.health, route events to an SNS topic, and configure the SNS topic to deliver to an AWS Chatbot channel connected to the Slack workspace.

options.label: D
options.text: Configure AWS Personal Health Dashboard to send email notifications and use an email-to-Slack bridge application to forward emails to the Slack channel.

distractors.A: RSS polling introduces delay and requires maintaining a Lambda function; EventBridge with Health events is push-based and near-real-time without custom code.
distractors.D: Email-to-Slack bridges are fragile and require external services; the native EventBridge + AWS Chatbot integration is the managed AWS approach.
distractors.B: AWS Health does not have a built-in Slack webhook configuration; the EventBridge + SNS + AWS Chatbot pipeline is the supported integration path.

explanation: AWS Health publishes account-specific events to EventBridge. An EventBridge rule matching {source: [aws.health]} captures all health events for the account (scheduled changes, issues, and notifications). Routing to SNS and then to AWS Chatbot (which connects to Slack) delivers formatted notifications to a Slack channel without any custom code.

stem: A SysOps administrator creates a CloudWatch alarm with a period of 60 seconds and a data points to alarm setting of 3 out of 5. When does the alarm transition to ALARM state?

options.label: A
options.text: The alarm transitions to ALARM after the metric has breached the threshold for 3 consecutive minutes out of any 5-minute window, then resets and starts counting again.

options.label: B
options.text: The alarm transitions to ALARM when the average of all 5 data points exceeds the threshold and at least 3 of those points individually breach the threshold.

options.label: C
options.text: The alarm transitions to ALARM when at least 3 of the most recent 5 one-minute data points breach the threshold, providing a more noise-resistant alert than requiring consecutive breaching points.

options.label: D
options.text: The alarm transitions to ALARM after the first 3 data points breach the threshold and then waits 5 minutes before re-evaluating to prevent rapid state changes.

distractors.A: The M-of-N evaluation is not reset after reaching the threshold; it is a rolling window evaluation where each new data point slides the window forward.
distractors.B: CloudWatch does not compute an average of N points and then check individual points separately; the M-of-N setting evaluates each point independently against the threshold.
distractors.D: There is no 5-minute re-evaluation delay after transitioning to ALARM; the alarm continuously evaluates each new data point.

explanation: The M out of N data points alarm configuration ('3 out of 5') means the alarm transitions to ALARM when M (3) of the most recent N (5) data points breach the threshold. This rolling window approach allows sporadic spikes to not trigger the alarm while still catching sustained problems. Each new 60-second data point slides the 5-point window forward.

stem: A SysOps administrator needs to forward AWS Config configuration change notifications to a downstream compliance system. What is the most direct integration?

options.label: A
options.text: Create an EventBridge rule matching Config events of type AWS API Call via CloudTrail for config-related API calls, then route to an SQS queue that the compliance system polls.

options.label: B
options.text: Enable Config streaming to a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream, which delivers configuration change records to an S3 bucket that the compliance system reads hourly.

options.label: C
options.text: Use the Config API's DescribeConfigurationRecorders operation on a schedule to retrieve the latest configuration changes and push them to the compliance system.

options.label: D
options.text: Configure an AWS Config delivery channel with an SNS topic; Config publishes configuration change notifications to the SNS topic, which can fan out to SQS queues, Lambda functions, or HTTP endpoints consumed by the compliance system.

distractors.A: EventBridge can match Config compliance change events, but for general configuration change notifications, the Config delivery channel SNS integration is the purpose-built mechanism.
distractors.B: AWS Config does not have native Kinesis Firehose streaming; the delivery channel supports S3 and SNS as delivery targets.
distractors.C: DescribeConfigurationRecorders returns information about the recorders themselves, not individual configuration item changes; using it for polling would require querying each resource type separately.

explanation: AWS Config delivery channels deliver configuration change notifications to an SNS topic in near-real-time. The SNS topic can then fan out to SQS for reliable delivery to the compliance system, to Lambda for real-time processing, or to HTTPS endpoints. This is the native mechanism Config provides for downstream notification of configuration changes.

stem: A company is running a containerized application on Amazon EKS. A SysOps administrator needs to collect pod-level CPU and memory metrics and send them to CloudWatch. Which solution requires the least custom development?

options.label: A
options.text: Deploy Prometheus in the EKS cluster and configure a custom exporter that scrapes pod metrics and posts them to CloudWatch using the PutMetricData API.

options.label: B
options.text: Deploy the CloudWatch Container Insights for EKS using the CloudWatch agent as a DaemonSet; it collects pod, node, and cluster metrics and sends them to CloudWatch without custom code.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable the Kubernetes Metrics Server in the EKS cluster; the Metrics Server publishes pod CPU and memory metrics directly to CloudWatch without additional configuration.

options.label: D
options.text: Configure the EKS managed node group to automatically forward container metrics to CloudWatch using the built-in node-level telemetry agent.

distractors.A: Prometheus with a custom exporter requires writing exporter code and managing Prometheus; CloudWatch Container Insights is a managed alternative that requires only deployment of the CloudWatch agent DaemonSet.
distractors.C: The Kubernetes Metrics Server provides in-cluster metrics for Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and kubectl top; it does not publish metrics to CloudWatch.
distractors.D: EKS managed node groups do not have a built-in telemetry agent that forwards container metrics to CloudWatch; Container Insights requires explicit deployment.

explanation: CloudWatch Container Insights for Amazon EKS deploys the CloudWatch agent as a DaemonSet on each node. It collects CPU, memory, disk, and network metrics at the pod, container, node, and cluster level and publishes them to CloudWatch in the ContainerInsights namespace. AWS provides the deployment manifest; no custom code is required.

stem: A SysOps administrator needs to reduce the volume of CloudWatch Logs data stored to cut costs while retaining error-level logs indefinitely. What is the most direct configuration?

options.label: A
options.text: Set a log retention policy on the log group to automatically expire and delete log events older than a defined period, such as 30 days, while separately routing error logs to a log group with no expiration.

options.label: B
options.text: Configure the CloudWatch agent to filter out non-error logs on the instance before sending them to CloudWatch, reducing the volume ingested.

options.label: C
options.text: Enable log compression on the CloudWatch Logs log group; compressed logs cost 60% less to store than uncompressed logs.

options.label: D
options.text: Export the log group to S3 monthly and delete the CloudWatch Logs data; S3 storage is cheaper and S3 Lifecycle rules manage long-term retention.

distractors.C: CloudWatch Logs does not offer a compression option that reduces storage cost; logs are stored and billed at their ingested size.
distractors.B: CloudWatch agent filtering can reduce ingestion volume, but it permanently discards the non-error logs; the retention policy approach keeps all logs for a defined period and then expires them.
distractors.D: Exporting to S3 is valid for long-term archival but requires a separate export job and log group management process; setting retention policies is simpler for reducing CloudWatch storage costs.

explanation: CloudWatch Logs retention policies define how long log events are kept in a log group before being automatically deleted. By setting a 30-day retention on the general log group and no expiration (Never) on a separate error-only log group, you retain all logs for 30 days for debugging while keeping error logs indefinitely for compliance, optimizing storage costs.

stem: A SysOps administrator needs to test whether a CloudWatch alarm action is working without waiting for the metric to naturally breach the threshold. What is the fastest approach?

options.label: A
options.text: Create a test metric filter that always matches and publishes a high value, causing the alarm to transition to ALARM state within the next evaluation period.

options.label: B
options.text: Use the CloudWatch set-alarm-state AWS CLI command to manually transition the alarm to ALARM state; this triggers all configured alarm actions for testing.

options.label: C
options.text: Configure the alarm with a 1-minute period and trigger a temporary spike in the monitored resource to cause a natural alarm breach for testing purposes.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the CloudWatch PutMetricData API to publish a high metric value that exceeds the alarm threshold; the alarm will breach on the next evaluation cycle.

distractors.A: Creating a test metric filter requires modifying the CloudWatch Logs configuration, is more complex, and introduces data into the metric that could skew historical analysis.
distractors.D: Publishing a high metric value via PutMetricData will eventually trigger the alarm, but it requires waiting for the evaluation period and adds test data points to the metric history.
distractors.C: Triggering a natural spike may cause real disruption to the application or service being monitored; set-alarm-state is safe and immediate.

explanation: The AWS CLI command 'aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state --alarm-name NAME --state-value ALARM --state-reason Testing' immediately transitions the alarm to ALARM state without modifying the underlying metric data. All configured alarm actions (SNS notifications, EC2 actions, Auto Scaling actions) are triggered. The alarm automatically returns to its correct state on the next metric evaluation.
